# Project overview

This logbook documents the construction of our replication and extension of
Hausmann and Sturzenegger (2006), *Global Imbalances or Bad Accounting? The
Missing Dark Matter in the Wealth of Nations*.

The project began as a replication exercise for the original H&S paper and
progressively evolved into an extension of the framework to the post-2003 global
financial system. The final version is organised around three blocks:

1. replication of the original H&S results;
2. extension of the analysis to 2022 and decomposition of net investment income
   by asset class;
3. original mechanism tests on intangibles, global risk, geopolitical risk and
   financial development.

The central idea of the project is to ask whether official current-account and
net international investment position data understate countries' true
income-generating external wealth. Following H&S, we infer an income-implied
external position by capitalising net investment income at a constant rate:

\[
NFA^{DM}_t = \frac{NII_t}{r}, \qquad r = 0.05.
\]

Dark matter is then defined as the gap between this income-implied net foreign
asset position and official NIIP:

\[
DM_t = NFA^{DM}_t - NIIP^{off}_t.
\]

The final interpretation is deliberately cautious: dark matter should not be
read as one single hidden stock of assets. It is better understood as a layered
residual combining return differentials, safe-asset services, portfolio
composition, FDI mismeasurement, intangible rents and multinational accounting.

# Part I — Replication of Hausmann & Sturzenegger (2006)

## Objective

The first objective was to reproduce the main empirical results of Hausmann and
Sturzenegger (2006). The original paper argues that official external accounts
systematically understate the true external wealth of countries like the United
States because they fail to capture income-generating assets that do not appear
in standard statistics.

The motivating puzzle is the United States. Between 1982 and 2005, the US
accumulated more than five trillion dollars in cumulative current-account
deficits. Under standard accounting, this should have made the US a large net
debtor paying substantial net investment income to the rest of the world.
Instead, US net investment income remained close to zero and often positive.

The first task was therefore to replicate:

- the US cumulative current-account and net investment income puzzle;
- the income-implied NFA measure;
- the cross-country offset mechanism;
- the determinant regressions for dark matter exports.

## Data assembled

We assembled the following datasets for the original replication period
1975--2005:

| Source | Use |
|---|---|
| IMF Balance of Payments | Current account balance and net primary income / net investment income |
| External Wealth of Nations, Brookings 2024 update | Official net foreign asset positions, FDI assets and liabilities |
| World Bank WDI | Constant-price GDP for HP filtering, R&D expenditure |
| World Governance Indicators | Rule of Law, averaged over 1996--2005 |
| Hard-coded country groups | OPEC and HIPC dummies from the original H&S appendix |

The use of the 2024 EWN update is important. It improves coverage and updates
historical series, but it also creates differences relative to the original
2006 data used by H&S.

## Construction of dark matter

For each country and year, we compute:

\[
NFA^{DM}_t = \frac{NII_t}{0.05}
\]

and

\[
CA^{DM}_t = NFA^{DM}_t - NFA^{DM}_{t-1}.
\]

Dark matter exports are defined as:

\[
XDM_t = CA^{DM}_t - CA^{off}_t.
\]

For the United States, we reconstruct the official NFA path by anchoring the
series at the BEA-reported 1982 value of 329 billion dollars and rolling it
forward and backward using current-account flows. Capital gains are excluded,
following the logic of the original paper.

## Output volatility

Output volatility is computed as the standard deviation of the HP-filtered log
real GDP cycle, with annual smoothing parameter:

\[
\lambda = 100.
\]

This variable proxies the insurance channel: stable economies should be able to
provide insurance services to more volatile economies and earn an implicit
premium.

## Figures replicated

The first replication stage generated the following figures:

- **Figure 1**: US cumulative current account vs. net investment income,
  1982--2005.
- **Figures 3a and 3b**: cumulative official current account vs.
  dark-matter-implied NFA change, with and without the US outlier.
- **Figure 5b**: dark matter exports vs. cumulative official current account,
  both as a share of 2003 GDP.
- **Figure 6c**: regional NFA positions including dark matter, as a share of
  world GDP.
- **Figure 8**: US dark matter stock in trillions of dollars and as a share of
  GDP, 1982--2005.

The most important visual result is the negative cross-country relationship
between official current-account balances and dark matter exports. This is the
core H&S offset mechanism.

## Tables replicated

The first replication stage also generated:

- **Table 1**: official cumulative current account regressed on the
  dark-matter-implied current account;
- **Table 2**: dark matter exports regressed on official cumulative current
  account;
- **Table 3**: cross-sectional determinants of dark matter exports;
- **Table 4 / 4b**: panel versions of the determinant regressions.

## Sample restriction issue

A major early issue was sample size. Initial regressions used far more countries
than the original paper because the EWN 2024 dataset covers many more countries
than the data available to H&S in 2006. This generated samples such as 170+
countries, whereas H&S used specific 109-country, 79-country and
industrial-country samples.

We fixed this by hard-coding the H&S country lists from Appendix A.2:

- 109-country broad sample for Tables 1 and 2;
- 79-country full-data sample for Table 3;
- 21-country industrial sample for industrial-country specifications.

After restriction, effective sample sizes were close to the original paper,
with remaining differences due to missing data in the updated IMF and EWN
series.

## WDI vs. IFS GDP for output volatility

We compared two sources for GDP in the HP-filtered output volatility measure:

1. World Bank WDI constant-price GDP;
2. IMF IFS quarterly GDP, aggregated to annual frequency.

Switching to IFS improved some coefficients, especially the Table 3 FDI
liabilities coefficient in column (i), but it worsened other results,
especially the panel Table 4 coefficients. It also reduced explanatory power in
some cross-sectional regressions.

We therefore kept WDI as the main GDP source. The rationale was that WDI gave
more stable overall results, performed better in the panel specifications and
was more consistent with the broader data strategy.

## Remaining divergences from H&S

After all fixes, three main divergences remained:

1. Output volatility sometimes had a different sign or weaker behaviour than in
   the original paper.
2. The FDI assets coefficient in panel specifications did not perfectly match
   H&S.
3. Table 1 coefficients were somewhat attenuated relative to the original paper.

We interpret these as legitimate replication limits rather than coding errors.
They are plausibly driven by:

- the 2024 revision of EWN external wealth data;
- different BOP coverage relative to the original paper;
- revised FDI stocks and valuation methods;
- country coverage changes;
- the increased importance of financial centres, special purpose entities and
  phantom FDI.

# Part II — Extension to 2022 and asset-class decomposition

## Motivation

The second part asks whether the H&S framework survives after the original
sample period. The original paper ends before several major events:

- the global financial crisis;
- the euro-area crisis;
- the rise of China as a major creditor;
- the COVID period;
- the expansion of multinational profit shifting and phantom FDI.

This makes the post-2003 extension important. If the offset mechanism only
holds before 2003, then dark matter may be a period-specific artifact. If it
survives to 2022, the H&S insight remains empirically relevant.

## Time update to 2022

We extend the original 5% capitalisation method to the 1980--2022 period using
updated IMF BOP and EWN data.

The most important result is the extended version of the H&S offset regression:

\[
XDM_i = \alpha + \beta CA_i^{off} + \varepsilon_i.
\]

The estimated coefficient is approximately:

\[
\hat{\beta} \simeq -0.94,
\]

with an \(R^2\) around 0.56. This is slightly stronger than the original-period
estimate around -0.885.

The interpretation is clear: countries with larger official current-account
surpluses tend to import dark matter, while countries with official deficits
tend to export it. The central offset mechanism survives the longer sample.

## Extended US dark matter stock

The US dark matter stock remains economically large after the original H&S
sample. In dollar terms, it continues to grow after 2005 and remains large
through the 2010s.

However, as a share of GDP, the US dark matter stock appears to decline after
the late 2010s. This is important for interpretation: the US advantage remains
large, but it is not mechanically increasing forever.

## Global NFA including dark matter

The updated global NFA figure shows that the United States still looks much
stronger under income-implied accounting than under official NIIP statistics.
Japan also remains creditor-like in income-implied terms.

However, the extended global picture is less stable than the original H&S
1980--2004 picture. The rest of the world becomes increasingly negative in the
dark-matter-adjusted decomposition. This suggests that income-implied global
imbalances may have become more pronounced in the post-2003 period.

## Insurance-channel decomposition: beta vs. idiosyncratic volatility

We explored a further extension of the H&S insurance channel. H&S use output
volatility as a single variable, but this mixes two forms of risk:

1. systematic exposure to world output fluctuations;
2. idiosyncratic country-specific volatility.

Theoretically, if dark matter reflects a globally priced insurance service,
then systematic beta with world output should matter more than purely domestic
idiosyncratic volatility.

We constructed:

- a rolling ten-year beta of each country's GDP growth with respect to world GDP
  growth;
- an idiosyncratic volatility measure based on the residuals of the same rolling
  regression.

The results were nuanced. The original H&S output volatility result survives in
the extended cross-section. However, once volatility is decomposed, the evidence
points more strongly to idiosyncratic volatility than to beta with world output.
In annual panel regressions, neither beta nor idiosyncratic volatility robustly
explains dark matter exports.

This weakens a clean global-insurance interpretation and suggests that the
strongest evidence remains cross-sectional rather than within-country over time.

## Asset-class decomposition

The most important methodological extension is the decomposition of net
investment income by asset class. The flat 5% capitalisation rate is useful as
a benchmark, but it treats very different income streams as if they had the
same risk and liquidity.

We therefore decompose NII into:

\[
j \in \{FDI, equity, debt, other\}.
\]

The component-specific implied NFA is:

\[
NFA^{comp}_t = \sum_j \frac{NII^j_t}{r_j}.
\]

The goal is not to build a full structural valuation model. It is to test
whether the H&S result survives when different income streams are treated
according to their economic nature.

## Scenario A: universal asset-class rates

Scenario A assigns common rates across countries:

- FDI: 8%;
- portfolio equity: 6%;
- portfolio debt: 3%;
- other investment income: 5%.

This keeps global comparability while acknowledging that FDI, equity and debt
should not be capitalised in the same way.

## Scenario B: country-group-specific rates

Scenario B allows rates to differ across country groups:

- privilege countries, such as the US, UK and Switzerland;
- other advanced economies;
- emerging economies.

This scenario captures the idea that some countries can issue safe and liquid
debt at lower yields, while emerging economies face higher debt premia.

A key methodological clarification emerged during writing: Scenario B must be
interpreted carefully because it still capitalises **net** income flows. If net
debt income is negative, a lower debt discount rate makes that component more
negative, not more positive. This is why Scenario C became central.

## Scenario C: gross-position approach

Scenario C separates gross external assets and liabilities:

\[
NFA^C_t = \frac{1}{r^{disc}}\sum_j
\left(A^j_t r^{j,A} - L^j_t r^{j,L}\right).
\]

This is the most conceptually transparent scenario because it directly measures
the return wedge between what a country earns on external assets and what it
pays on external liabilities.

It makes the exorbitant-privilege mechanism explicit:

- the United States earns high returns on outward FDI and equity;
- it pays low returns on safe and liquid debt liabilities;
- China holds large low-yielding assets while paying relatively high returns on
  inward FDI liabilities.

This changes the interpretation of dark matter. It is not just about whether a
country is a creditor or debtor. It is about the composition and return profile
of its external balance sheet.

# Part III — Original economic extensions

## General objective

The third part moves beyond replication and asks what dark matter captures in
the post-2003 global financial system. The objective is not to find one single
mechanism, but to assess which channels remain informative once the H&S residual
is brought to modern data.

The extensions test:

- intangible capital;
- global financial risk;
- geopolitical risk;
- financial development;
- asset-class composition.

## Extension 1 — Safe-asset cycle and VIX

The first mechanism test focuses on the insurance or safe-asset interpretation.
If safe havens provide insurance to global investors, then the value of this
service should rise when global risk aversion increases.

We use annual changes in log VIX as a proxy for global financial risk. The
empirical strategy estimates whether safe-haven economies react differently to
VIX shocks than other countries.

The main result is not a simple confirmation of the safe-asset premium. The
safe-haven interaction is negative under the H&S 5% method and weaker under the
component-specific method. This suggests that safe havens do not necessarily
record higher annual dark matter exports when the VIX rises.

The interpretation is closer to "exorbitant duty": in crises, safe havens
provide liquidity and insurance, but the payoff may appear through lower
funding costs, capital gains or balance-sheet effects rather than immediate
annual NII.

## Extension 1b — Financial risk vs. geopolitical risk

We then distinguish financial risk from geopolitical risk. The VIX captures
financial-market stress, while the Caldara-Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk index
captures geopolitical uncertainty.

The horse-race specification includes both VIX and GPR interactions. The VIX
safe-haven interaction remains more stable than the GPR interaction. GPR is
weaker and loses significance once VIX is controlled for.

The conclusion is that dark matter responds more clearly to global financial
risk than to geopolitical news in annual data.

## Extension 2 — Intangible capital intensity

H&S proxy the knowledge-capital channel with R&D. We broaden this idea using a
composite intangible index based on:

- R&D expenditure;
- resident patent applications;
- high-technology exports;
- ICT service exports.

The intuition is that modern intangible capital is multidimensional and may be
poorly captured by R&D alone.

The result is negative but informative. R&D and the broader intangible index do
not robustly predict dark matter exports. This does not rule out intangible
rents. Instead, it suggests that aggregate country-level proxies cannot easily
separate countries producing intangible assets from countries hosting
multinational profits for tax or accounting reasons.

## Extension 3 — Financial development and safe-asset production

The safe-asset literature suggests that countries with deeper financial markets
may be better able to produce internationally demanded safe assets. We therefore
construct a financial development index using:

- private credit to GDP;
- stock market capitalisation to GDP.

Financial development is not a robust positive predictor of dark matter. The
composite index is weakly negative in one specification and becomes
insignificant with broader controls. Output volatility remains more robust.

The interpretation is that safe-asset production is not simply a matter of
domestic financial depth. Reserve-currency status, legal credibility, market
liquidity, geopolitical power and network externalities likely matter more.

## Extension 4 — NII composition by asset class

Finally, we look directly at observed net investment income composition. This
is not a descriptive add-on: it is necessary for interpreting what the dark
matter residual measures.

The same aggregate NII can come from very different channels:

- FDI rents;
- portfolio equity returns;
- debt income;
- other investment income;
- multinational profit recording;
- financial-centre pass-through.

The US--China contrast is especially informative:

- the US has a negative official NIIP but strong income generation because its
  external assets are tilted toward high-return FDI and equity while its
  liabilities include safe low-yield debt;
- China has a positive official NIIP, but weaker income generation because it
  holds low-yielding external assets and pays relatively high returns on inward
  FDI liabilities.

This supports the portfolio-composition interpretation of dark matter.

# Literature positioning

## Exorbitant privilege and return differentials

The extension to 2022 connects directly to the exorbitant-privilege literature.
Gourinchas and Rey show that the United States earns higher returns on external
assets than it pays on external liabilities. This shifts the interpretation of
US dark matter from a mysterious hidden stock toward a persistent return
advantage.

This is consistent with our extended results: the US remains much stronger
under income-implied accounting, but the advantage is not mechanically
unlimited.

## Exorbitant duty and safe assets

Gourinchas, Rey and Govillot develop the idea of "exorbitant duty": the US may
earn a privilege in normal times but also provide insurance to the rest of the
world during crises.

This supports our VIX extension. However, our results show that crisis periods
do not necessarily generate higher contemporaneous dark matter exports for safe
havens. The benefit may appear through funding costs, valuation effects or the
ability to issue safe liabilities.

## Global financial cycle

The VIX extension also connects with the Global Financial Cycle literature.
Miranda-Agrippino and Rey show that a global factor explains a significant
share of international risky asset price variation. This justifies using the
VIX as a proxy for global financial stress.

## Geopolitical risk

The GPR extension draws on Caldara and Iacoviello's index of geopolitical risk.
It allows us to distinguish financial stress from broader geopolitical
instability. Our results suggest that the dark matter mechanism is more closely
linked to financial-market stress than to geopolitical risk in annual data.

## Intangible capital

The intangible-capital extension is motivated by Corrado, Hulten and Sichel,
who argue that standard national accounts omit important forms of intangible
investment, including software, organisational capital and brand equity.

This supports the idea that H&S's R&D proxy is too narrow. However, our broader
intangible index still does not robustly explain dark matter exports, likely
because modern multinational accounting and profit shifting blur the geography
of intangible rents.

## Profit shifting and phantom FDI

The most important post-H&S qualification comes from the literature on tax
havens, profit shifting and measurement error. Work by Wright and Zucman,
Tørsløv, Wier and Zucman, Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen, and Coppola et al.
suggests that cross-border returns and external positions are heavily affected
by tax-haven subsidiaries, phantom FDI and the residence-based structure of
international statistics.

This means that some dark matter may reflect productive know-how or insurance
services, but some may also reflect statistical and accounting conventions.

# Final synthesis

The final project supports the broad H&S insight: official external accounts
can be misleading because they do not fully capture income-generating external
positions.

However, the meaning of dark matter changes once the sample is extended and the
residual is decomposed. It is not one hidden stock of assets. It is a diagnostic
residual combining:

- return privilege;
- safe-asset demand;
- insurance services;
- FDI mismeasurement;
- intangible rents;
- profit shifting;
- financial-centre pass-through;
- statistical conventions.

The strongest empirical result remains the offset mechanism: official
current-account imbalances are systematically offset by dark matter exports.
The most robust mechanism is the insurance/stability channel, although it is
clearer in cross-section than in annual panel variation. The asset-class
decomposition provides the most useful interpretation of why countries with
similar official net positions can have very different income-generating
capacity.

# Practical lessons from the project

## Data lessons

- Replications using modern data can differ substantially from original papers
  because datasets are revised.
- Sample restriction is crucial. Using all currently available countries can
  change the exercise completely.
- FDI data are especially sensitive to revisions, financial centres, special
  purpose entities and profit shifting.
- Cross-sectional cumulative results are more stable than annual panel results.

## Methodological lessons

- The flat 5% capitalisation rate is useful for comparability but too coarse for
  interpretation.
- Asset-class decomposition is essential for distinguishing FDI rents from
  safe-asset effects.
- Gross-position analysis is preferable when studying return privilege.
- Mechanism tests should be interpreted as suggestive rather than causal.
